renderSubtitles.text:
An engine turns a straight push into a spin, with just three
parts: a piston, a connecting rod, and a crankshaft.

The piston can only slide along its cylinder. The crank can
only turn about its shaft. The rod ties the two together.

Turn the crank one full revolution, and
the piston goes out and back, once.

The crank pin travels in a circle. The piston is held to
a straight line. A rod of fixed length joins them.

Where the piston turns around are the dead
centers: top dead center, and bottom dead center.

The distance between them is the stroke. It
is exactly twice the crank's radius.

Notice the piston is not simple back and forth. A
quarter turn from the top, it is already past halfway.

Now orbit the assembly. The crank pin sits between two webs, the
rod wraps the pin, and the piston turns on the other end.

Push the piston with a steady force. Extend the rod's line to
the shaft: the gold gap is the leverage the crank gets.

At a dead center, the line runs straight through the shaft, and the
leverage is zero. Near the middle of the stroke, it is the greatest.

That is why an engine needs a heavy flywheel: its
weight carries the crank through the dead centers.

Crank-slider kinematics: a circle, a line, and a
rod of fixed length. Everything else follows.
